item.title: Drug Therapies and Incidence of Dementia Among Adults With Overactive Bladder
item.description:
Importance: Concern that anticholinergic medications for overactive bladder (OAB) are associated with increased dementia risk has encouraged a shift toward β3 adrenergic agonists, which are presumed cognitively safer. Whether this presumption is justified is uncertain.

Objective: To compare the risk of incident dementia among adults initiating high-risk anticholinergic, low-risk anticholinergic, or β3 agonist therapy for OAB and to evaluate the association of treatment duration with risk.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study used Epic Cosmos electronic health record data from 2012 to 2025. Adults aged 40 to 90 years newly treated for OAB within 1 year of diagnosis without preexisting dementia were included.

Exposures: First prescribed medication class: high-risk anticholinergics (oxybutynin, tolterodine, or solifenacin), low-risk anticholinergics (darifenacin, trospium, or fesoterodine), or β3 agonists (mirabegron or vibegron).

Main outcomes and measures: Incident dementia by diagnosis code or dementia-specific medication. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and Cox proportional hazards models were used, with analyses stratified by age and sex and an exploratory landmark duration-response analysis.

Results: Among 830 393 patients (585 198 female [70.5%]; median [IQR] age, 67 [57-76] years), incident dementia occurred in 65 134 patients, with a median (IQR) follow-up ranging from 1046 (571-1809) days for β3 agonists to 1568 (857-2614) days for high-risk anticholinergics. After IPTW, high-risk anticholinergics were associated with a lower hazard of dementia than β3 agonists (hazard ratio [HR], 0.90; 95% CI, 0.87-0.93) and low-risk anticholinergics (HR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.90-0.96); low-risk anticholinergics did not differ from β3 agonists (HR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.93-1.01). Weighted 10-year dementia risk was highest for β3 agonists (20.0%; 95% CI, 18.8%-21.2%) and lowest for high-risk anticholinergics (18.1%; 95% CI, 17.9%-18.3%). E-values of 1.29 (high-risk anticholinergics vs β3 agonists) and 1.20 (high-risk vs low-risk anticholinergics) suggested that observed differences could be explained by a modest amount of unmeasured confounding. Longer anticholinergic duration was not associated with increased risk.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of patients undergoing treatment for OAB, β3 agonists were not associated with a lower dementia incidence compared with anticholinergics. These findings suggest that previously reported increases in risk may reflect residual confounding rather than a pharmacological effect.

item.title: A Scalable Teacher Professional Development and Wellness Program in Primary Schools: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: In Uganda and other low-income settings with prevalent mental health problems and limited resources, scalable professional development (PD) models are needed to strengthen teachers' capacity to apply evidence-based practices to support child mental health.

Objective: To examine the short-term effectiveness of PD and PD with a teacher-wellness enhancement (PDT) compared with a control condition on teacher knowledge and use of evidence-based practices, teacher stress, and teacher stress management; implementation outcomes; and the differential outcomes between urban and rural primary schools in Uganda.

Design, setting, and participants: This cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted in 47 urban and rural schools in Uganda between August 2021 and February 2025. Participating teachers in the schools were followed-up 24 months after the intervention, and the present trial focused on short-term teacher outcomes. Statistical analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle.

Interventions: Schools and teachers were randomized to 1 of 3 conditions: PD, PDT, and control. The PD intervention (mWEL-PD or Mental Wellbeing and Empowering Lives of the School Community: Professional Development) consisted of 3 days of training and 8 one-hour coaching sessions in person for 2 to 3 months. The PDT intervention (mWEL-PD with a teacher-wellness enhancement) was provided as the PD program plus a 1-day workshop and 3 group support sessions. The control condition offered no intervention during year 1, but mental health knowledge and promotion materials and a 1-day teacher-wellness workshop were provided in year 2.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcomes for PD and PDT groups were knowledge and use of evidence-based practices. Teachers completed 15 self-report measures assessing 4 key outcomes: knowledge of evidence-based practices, use of evidence-based practices, teacher stress, and teacher stress management. Implementation outcomes, self-assessed after completion of the intervention, included teacher engagement in the intervention, teacher perception of acceptability and usefulness of the content, and teacher perception of the competence of the program facilitators.

Results: A total of 47 schools with 509 teachers (mean [SD] age, 40.60 [11.12] years; 368 females [72.3%]) were included in the analysis. Among the schools, 15 (31.9%) were randomly assigned to the control, 16 (34.0%) to the PD, and 16 (34.0%) to the PDT groups. Among teachers, 165 (32.4%) were randomly assigned to the control, 187 (36.7%) to the PD, and 157 (30.8%) to the PDT groups. Teacher attendance at training and coaching sessions and ratings of relevance and facilitator competence were high in both urban and rural contexts. Compared with teachers in the PD group, those in the PDT group were more likely to attend all training days offered (120 of 187 [64.1%] in the PD group vs 127 of 157 [80.9%] in the PDT group) and participated in more coaching sessions (mean [SD] number, 4.58 [2.91] vs 6.09 [2.28]). Compared with teachers in the control condition, teachers in the PDT condition benefited on all 4 key outcomes: increased knowledge (standardized mean difference [SMD], 0.57; 95% CI, 0.26-0.88) and use (SMD, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.01-0.71) of evidence-based practices, increased stress management (SMD, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.19-0.80), and decreased stress (SMD, -0.27; 95% CI, -0.54 to 0.01). Benefits of PD were limited to knowledge of evidence-based practices (SMD, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.03-0.62).

Conclusions and relevance: This trial of a scalable teacher PD program delivered through existing educational infrastructure and resources demonstrates the program's feasibility, acceptability, and impact on self-reported teacher outcomes. The finding of short-term benefits for teacher practice and wellness suggests the potential of the PDT model for school-based mental health promotion.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04383327.

item.title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Mammography Outcomes by Advanced Breast Cancer Risk
item.description:
Importance: Few studies have examined advanced breast cancer rates in women undergoing routine mammography and/or breast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

Objective: To compare screening outcomes of breast MRI vs mammography by advanced breast cancer risk and screening round.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study included women aged 40 to 74 years who had a screening MRI performed with or without a screening film, digital, or digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) mammogram within 12 months (MRI group) or a screening digital or DBT mammogram (mammography-only group) performed at breast imaging facilities participating in the Breast Cancer Surveillance Consortium (BCSC) between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2021, and breast cancers diagnosed between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2022. Data analysis was performed from April 2025 to August 2026.

Exposures: MRI and mammography; advanced breast cancer risk score calculated using the BCSC advanced cancer risk model and categorized as low (0% to <0.172%), average (0.172% to <0.3797%), intermediate (0.3797% to <0.6582%), or higher (≥0.6582%).

Main outcomes and measures: Advanced (prognostic stage II or higher) and screen-detected early-stage (prognostic stage I) invasive cancer and false-positive biopsy recommendation rates per 1000 examinations adjusting for registry, examination year, age, race and ethnicity, family history, prior breast biopsy, and breast density.

Results: A total of 172 865 examinations performed in 105 532 women (median [IQR] age, 52 [46-59] years) were studied. After mammography, the intermediate to high vs low to average risk group had significantly higher advanced cancer (0.6 vs 0.3; difference, 0.4; 95% CI, 0.1-0.6), screen-detected early-stage cancer (2.8 vs 1.8; difference, 1.1; 95% CI, 0.5-1.7), and false-positive biopsy recommendation (18.1 vs 14.7; difference, 3.4; 95% CI, 1.7-5.2) rates per 1000 examinations. In the MRI group, rates per 1000 examinations of advanced cancer (0.8 vs 1.1; difference, -0.3; 95% CI, -1.3 to 0.7), screen-detected early-stage disease (10.3 vs 11.4; difference, -1.1; 95% CI, -4.9 to 2.7), and false-positive biopsy recommendation (94.0 vs 93.3; difference, 0.7; 95% CI, -9.9 to 11.3) were not significantly different between intermediate to high and low to average advanced cancer risk groups. Advanced cancer rates were not significantly different for MRI vs mammography between risk groups (difference, 0.6; 95% CI, -0.4 to 1.6). Screen-detected early-stage rates were significantly higher for MRI vs mammography for low to average risk (11.4 vs 1.8; difference, 9.6; 95% CI, 7.3-12.0) and intermediate to high risk (10.3 vs 2.8; difference, 7.5; 95% CI, 4.9-10.1) groups as were false-positive biopsy recommendation rates for low to average risk (93.3 vs 14.7; difference, 78.6; 95% CI, 72.5-84.8) and intermediate to high risk (94.0 vs 18.1; difference, 75.9; 95% CI, 68.3-83.5) groups. Women who underwent subsequent vs first MRIs had significantly lower advanced cancer rates (0.4 vs 2.0; difference, 1.6; 95% CI, 0.3-2.8) and higher advanced cancer risk (median [IQR] BCSC advanced cancer risk score, 0.348 [0.238 to 0.490] vs 0.301 [0.213 to 0.429]; P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, intermediate to high advanced breast cancer risk was associated with higher advanced cancer rates with screening mammography. MRI screening was associated with higher screen-detected early-stage cancer rates compared with mammography but not lower advanced cancer rates, except among women who underwent repeat MRIs. These results suggest that women with elevated advanced cancer risk should discuss MRI screening with their physician.

item.title: Primary Endocrine Therapy vs Upfront Surgery for Older Women With Estrogen Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
item.description:
Importance: As the population of older women with breast cancer grows, an increasing number are considered for primary endocrine therapy (pET), yet clinicians lack a framework for identifying which patients are appropriate candidates, resulting in reliance on chronologic age and life expectancy rather than tumor biology.

Objective: To evaluate survival and variables associated with response duration for patients treated with pET.

Data sources: PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception through March 26, 2026.

Study selection: Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and non-RCT (observational) cohorts comparing pET with surgery in operable, nonmetastatic, estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer.

Data extraction and synthesis: Data were extracted independently by 2 reviewers per Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Hazard ratios (HRs) not directly reported were reconstructed from Kaplan-Meier curves. Randomized clinical trial-derived HRs for overall survival (OS) and breast cancer-specific survival (BCSS) were pooled using a random-effects model, given anticipated heterogeneity across trials spanning 5 decades and differing tumor biology criteria. Observational cohorts were analyzed descriptively, not pooled for comparative survival, given susceptibility to confounding by indication.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes were OS and BCSS (RCTs) assessed using meta-analysis. Time to progression, salvage intervention rates, and variables associated with progression and mortality (observational cohorts) were assessed using descriptive analyses.

Results: Twenty-nine studies (6 RCTs and 23 observational cohorts; 22 821 patients; overall median [IQR] age, 83.1 [77.0-85.0] years) met the inclusion criteria. Patients from RCTs were generally younger (median [IQR] age, 77.0 [75.8-78.0] years) than those from the observational studies (median [IQR] age, 84.0 [81.5-86.0] years). Treatment with pET was not associated with a statistically significant OS difference vs surgery (HR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.98-1.33), though the point estimate favored surgery. Median time to progression ranged from 19.7 months (range, 13.5-26.0 months) in tumor biology-unselected, tamoxifen-era cohorts to more than 50 months in ER-selected and aromatase inhibitor-treated cohorts. Tumor biology was consistently associated with progression risk.

Conclusions and relevance: This systematic review and meta-analysis of more than 22 000 patients with ER-positive breast cancer found no statistically significant survival difference between pET and upfront surgery. Durable disease control under pET seemed to be concentrated in patients with favorable biology. These findings support a framework incorporating tumor biology and frailty, rather than age alone, to identify candidates for pET.

item.title: State Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer and Food Insufficiency
item.description:
Importance: Children who receive free or reduced-price school meals often face increased hunger during the summer, when school-based meals are unavailable. Since 2024, states may opt into implementing the Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer (SEBT) program, which provides low-income families a one-time, federally funded grocery benefit of $120 per school-aged child.

Objective: To examine the association between state implementation of SEBT and subsequent household food insufficiency among SEBT-eligible, low-income households with school-aged children.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study used demographic and health data from January to September 2024 cycles of the nationally representative Household Pulse Survey conducted by the US Census Bureau. Eligible households included children aged 5 to 17 years who were eligible for SEBT based on reported Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) receipt and/or income 185% of the federal poverty level (FPL) or below. Data analysis was performed between April 2025 and August 2026.

Exposure: State-level implementation of SEBT between May and August 2024 (treated vs untreated states).

Main outcomes and measures: Household food insufficiency, measured by a respondent indicating they sometimes or often did not have enough food in their household during the previous 7 days.

Results: Among 31 059 SEBT-eligible households (1090 Asian [3.5%], 5692 Black [18.3%], 5845 Hispanic [18.8%], 21 166 White [68.1%]), the majority of households in both untreated (18 states) and treated (33 states, including District of Columbia) states had income below 185% FPL (10 233 [93.4%] and 17 105 [92.0%], respectively). Among 11 334 households in untreated states, 4392 received Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) (42.6%) and 1196 received Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) benefits (12.3%); among 19 725 households in treated states, 9512 (50.4%) received SNAP, and 2126 (12.3%) received WIC. Among low-income families (185% FPL or below) with school-aged children, household food insufficiency increased by 4.0 percentage points (95% CI, 2.1 to 5.9 percentage points) during the summer compared with nonsummer months. Only a mean (SD) 30.3% (8.3) of SEBT-eligible households in treated states reported receiving SEBT. State implementation of SEBT was not significantly associated with a change in food insufficiency among SEBT-eligible households (0.8 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.4 to 4.0 percentage points).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study, household food insufficiency increased significantly during summer months among low-income households of school-aged children and state implementation of SEBT was not significantly associated with a change in food insufficiency among SEBT-eligible households.

item.title: Molecular Testing Among Patients With Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer in the Rural US
item.description:
Importance: Molecular evaluation is standard of care for patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in the US. Patients in rural areas face disproportionate lung cancer mortality associated with reduced guideline-concordant evaluation and treatment receipt, but molecular testing patterns have not been described in this population.

Objective: To characterize molecular testing patterns in the rural US following initial testing implementation.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study used the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program linked to Medicare claims data to identify individuals aged 66 years or older diagnosed with advanced NSCLC from January 2014 to December 2019. Data analysis was performed from December 2025 to August 2026.

Exposures: Sociodemographic variables, histology, and practitioner visits.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was receipt of molecular testing. The cumulative incidence of testing overall and by patient subgroups defined at baseline were calculated using the total person-time at risk (30 days before diagnosis to death or 6 months after diagnosis) using a competing-risks framework, with death as the competing event.

Results: Among a total of 8259 Medicare beneficiaries residing in rural areas who were diagnosed with advanced NSCLC included in the study (mean [SD] age, 76.1 [6.7] years; 4672 males [56.6%]), 1775 (21.5%) were eligible for Medicaid, 3754 (45.5%) had adenocarcinoma histology, 2044 (24.7%) had squamous histology, and 2461 (29.8%) had other or unspecified histology. In the cohort, 2963 (35.9%) received molecular testing. The cumulative incidence of testing by 180 days after diagnosis was 0.36 (95% CI, 0.35-0.37). Increasing age (hazard ratio [HR], 0.96 [95% CI, 0.93-0.99]), later diagnosis year (HR, 1.05 [95% CI, 1.02-1.07]), dual Medicaid coverage (HR, 0.71 [95% CI, 0.64-0.79]), Part D enrollment (HR, 1.13 [95% CI, 1.04-1.22]), and squamous histology (HR, 0.35 [95% CI, 0.32-0.39]) were independently associated with testing. A greater percentage of patients who received testing had visits with both a proceduralist or a surgeon and an oncologist compared with those without testing (1257 [77.7%] vs 867 [58.9%]; P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of Medicare beneficiaries with advanced NSCLC residing in the rural US, initial receipt of molecular testing was low. Dual Medicaid coverage, Part D enrollment, and subspecialist visits were independently associated with test receipt, highlighting key areas for future study to promote equitable delivery of guideline-concordant lung cancer care.

item.title: Changes in Racial, Ethnic, and Gender Differences in Promotion and Retention Among US Medical School Clinical Faculty
item.description:
Importance: Understanding how racial-, ethnic-, and gender-based differences in academic promotion have changed over time is important for advancing equity in academic medicine.

Objective: To examine changes over time in racial-, ethnic-, and gender-based differences in promotion and attrition among academic clinical faculty.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study used deidentified data from the AAMC faculty roster for full-time faculty appointments between 1960 and 2024, based on an August 31, 2025, data snapshot.

Exposure: Race and ethnicity (categorized as American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander; Asian; Black; Hispanic; White; and other [any race or ethnicity not otherwise specified]), gender, and medical school graduation cohort (2000 or earlier vs after 2000).

Main outcomes and measures: Cox proportional hazards models were used to examine differences in promotion to associate professor, professor, and attrition by race, ethnicity, and gender across medical school graduation cohorts and were presented as adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs).

Results: Included were 289 129 physicians at 152 institutions (179 081 men [61.9%]; 1093 American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander [0.4%]; 62 403 Asian [21.6%]; 13 330 Black [4.6%]; 16 865 Hispanic [5.8%]; 3034 other [1.1%]; 192 404 White [66.6%]). Compared with White faculty, Black faculty were less likely to be promoted to associate professor overall; this difference narrowed over time (before 2000: aHR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.60-0.74; after 2000: aHR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.71-0.83; P for interaction = .01). The difference in promotion to professor between Black and White faculty also narrowed over time (before 2000: aHR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.77-0.94; after 2000: aHR, 1.09, 95% CI, 0.92-1.29; P for interaction = .02). Women were less likely than men to be promoted to associate professor, although this difference narrowed over time (before 2000: aHR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.77-0.82; after 2000: aHR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.85-0.98; P for interaction <.001). Women were less likely than men to be promoted to professor in both graduation cohorts, with no evidence of change over time (before 2000: aHR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.90-0.97; after 2000: aHR 0.91; 95% CI, 0.83-0.99; P for interaction = .48). Attrition was more likely among American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, or Pacific Islander (aHR, 1.25; 95% CI, 1.12-1.40), Asian (aHR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.04-1.10), Black (aHR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.14-1.25), Hispanic (aHR, 1.10; 95% CI, 1.05-1.15), and women (aHR, 1.11; 95% CI: 1.08-1.13) faculty than among White and men faculty.

Conclusions and relevance: In this retrospective cohort study of 289 129 physicians, Black faculty experienced less disparity in promotion over time, and disparities in promotion to associate professor also narrowed for women; however, women remained less likely to be promoted to professor, and attrition remained higher for all minoritized racial and ethnic groups and for women. These findings suggest incremental progress while underscoring the need for continued efforts to achieve greater diversity and equity within academic medicine.

item.title: Indoor Radon and Incident Heart Failure Among Postmenopausal Women
item.description:
Importance: Evidence has shown an association of radon exposure with heart failure risk factors, but whether there is an association with heart failure remains unclear.

Objective: To assess whether indoor radon concentrations are associated with incident heart failure among US postmenopausal women.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective cohort study used data from the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) observational study and clinical trials. Participants were postmenopausal women from 40 US clinical centers who were aged 50 to 79 years and did not have self-reported heart failure at enrollment or randomization (September 1993 to December 1998) but had physician adjudication of heart failure during follow-up through February 17, 2024.

Exposure: Geocoded participant address-based assignment of county-level, US Environmental Protection Agency-categorized indoor radon concentration (<2, 2-4, or >4 picocuries [pCi]/L).

Main outcome and measure: Incident hospitalization for acute decompensated heart failure was ascertained through physician adjudication of medical records. Hazard ratios (HRs) for heart failure by indoor radon concentration were estimated with Cox proportional hazards regression models.

Results: Among 43 188 postmenopausal women (mean [SD] age, 63 [7] years), 36% were exposed to a radon concentration less than 2 pCi/L; 41%, to a concentration of 2 to 4 pCi/L; and 23%, to a concentration of more than 4 pCi/L. Over a mean (SD) follow-up of 16.2 (8.4) years, 3446 incident heart failure events occurred. The fully adjusted HR for heart failure was 1.19 (95% CI, 1.07-1.33) at more than 4 pCi/L vs less than 2 pCi/L, changing little in sensitivity analyses. The HR was higher for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (1.24; 95% CI, 1.04-1.49) and heart failure mortality (1.37; 95% CI, 1.12-1.69) at radon concentrations more than 4 pCi/L vs less than 2 pCi/L, but these HRs were not different from the null at concentrations of 2 to 4 pCi/L vs less than 2 pCi/L. The HR at concentrations greater than 4 pCi/L approximated that of a 16-mm Hg increase in systolic blood pressure or an increase of 4.8 in body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of US postmenopausal women, higher indoor radon concentrations were associated with an increased risk of incident heart failure, suggesting that radon may be a modifiable environmental determinant of heart failure.

item.title: Distribution of Coal Power, Pollution, and Poverty
item.description:
Importance: The adverse social exposome-life-course exposure to harmful social-environmental conditions-is associated with poor health outcomes. Exposure to heavy metals in air pollution from coal-fired power plants (CPP) may represent an underlying mechanism of this disparity, yet the association between the US adverse social exposome measured with the Area Deprivation Index (ADI) and CPP remains unknown.

Objective: To characterize the populations and adverse social exposome (indexed by ADI) of communities neighboring operational CPP.

Design, setting, and participants: Cross-sectional study of the US population using data from the 2023 Neighborhood Atlas. Data were analyzed from March to April 2026.

Exposure: Proximity to CPP was operationalized using 4 circular buffer zones: 3, 10, 25, and 50 miles in radius.

Main outcomes and measures: (1) Characterize each buffer zone by ADI and (2) determine the potential population-level exposure to CPP. Census block group delineations and population characteristics are from time-concordant US Census and American Community Survey data.

Results: The 2023 US population included 335 563 144 people (169 517 541 [50.5%] female, 66 294 296 [19.8%] Hispanic, 269 268 846 [80.2%] not Hispanic or Latino, and 212 002 396 [63.1%] White). A total of 2 783 004 people (0.83% of the US population) lived within 3 miles of a CPP. This group was more likely to live in the highest ADI neighborhoods as compared with the lowest ADI neighborhoods. Compared with the US population, these individuals were more likely to be American Indian and Alaska Native, White, and non-Hispanic. Populations living in the lowest 10% of ADI neighborhoods (most advantaged) had lower odds (odds ratio, 0.04; 95% CI, 0.00-0.81) of living within 3 miles of a CPP as compared with populations living in the highest 10% of ADI neighborhoods (most disadvantaged).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of US communities' proximity to CPP, we found that neighborhoods potentially exposed to CPP's hazardous environmental toxicants were more likely to be high ADI (ie, lower socioeconomic status) than low ADI (ie, higher socioeconomic status), highlighting the significantly greater burden of environmental toxicants potentially borne by disadvantaged US populations. Recent federal deregulations are likely to further increase these potential CPP-related toxin exposures. Additional study is needed to determine if these environmental toxicants trigger biological mechanisms underpinning the association between high ADI and poor health.

item.title: US Medical Education Reform Reports, 1910 to 2024
item.description:
Importance: Since the early 20th century, prominent private foundations, medical organizations, and government agencies have published reports calling for reform of medical education; however, it is unclear whether these reports contain repetitive messages about improving medical education, are a source of curriculum improvement, and are an antidote to medical education inertia.

Objective: To replicate and amplify findings of a similar analysis of reports published between 1910 and 1993 that advocated for reform in medical education using reports published from 1995 to 2024 and to identify recurring themes and potential sources of inertia in medical education.

Evidence review: PubMed, Scopus, Education Resources Information Center, and Google were searched on February 4, February 13, and March 19, 2025, using search terms addressing medical education, reform, and recommendations to identify reports on reform in medical education. A descriptive and interpretive content analysis of the medical education reports spanning 114 years was conducted from February 2025 to May 2026.

Findings: A total of 47 reports, including 19 analyzed in the previous study, were identified and analyzed. Consistent coding of content in the 47 reports was achieved. One of 4 core reform objectives of medical education, serve changing public interest, increased in endorsement over time. The other 3 core objectives-address physician workforce needs, cope with burgeoning knowledge, foster generalism-decreased or were unchanged. Four secondary reform objectives-apply new educational methods, address the changing nature of illness burden, address the changing nature of practice, increase quality and standards of education-increased in prevalence. Proposed methods of educational reform varied over 114 years, shaped by conceptual updates and technology advancements. None of the reports expressed criticism of traditional apprenticeship clinical education. Few reports displayed knowledge or awareness of the science of expertise in medical education.

Conclusions and relevance: In this study of medical education reports issued over 114 years, 3 basic values emerged: reform medical education, affirm core social and professional values, and protect the profession from outside intrusion. Proposed reform objectives and the means to achieve them displayed both stability and change longitudinally. The time-honored apprenticeship approach to clinical education was unquestioned. Despite a growing body of evidence from the science of expertise, proposed medical education reforms have produced insignificant curriculum change.

item.title: RELAX Perinatal Digital Intervention to Prevent Increasing Anxiety: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Anxiety disorders affect 1 in 5 pregnant women and birthing people. Cognitive bias modification for interpretation reduces anxiety and repetitive negative thinking (RNT; a risk factor for anxiety) among nonpregnant samples.

Objective: To evaluate whether adding pregnancy-tailored cognitive bias modification for interpretation to usual maternity care (UC) prevents increased anxiety during pregnancy; reduces anxiety, depression, and RNT before and after birth; and improves functioning before and after birth compared with UC.

Design, setting, and participants: The RELAX (Reducing Levels of Anxiety) 2-arm, parallel-group, multisite, superiority, phase 2b randomized clinical trial recruited participants from June 2023 to July 2024, with final assessment in April 2025. Participants included pregnant individuals in the UK at 16 to 28 weeks' gestation, with high RNT and up to moderate anxiety, recruited via antenatal clinics or self-referral.

Intervention: Participants were randomized to the self-led digital intervention (RELAX plus UC), involving twelve 17-minute sessions over 4 weeks, or to UC.

Main outcomes and measures: Assessments took place at baseline before randomization (T0) and 4 weeks (T1), 8 weeks (T2), and 36 weeks (T3; 12-24 weeks after birth) after randomization. The primary outcome was anxiety, as assessed by the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7) at T2 and as a secondary outcome at T3. Secondary outcomes included RNT (assessed by the 10-item trait version of the Repetitive Thinking Questionnaire [RTQ-10]), depression (general and perinatal, assessed by the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 [PHQ-9] and Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale [EPDS]), perinatal anxiety (assessed by the Perinatal Anxiety Screening Scale [PASS]), worry (assessed by the Penn State Worry Questionnaire [PSWQ]), and functioning (assessed by the Work and Social Adjustment Scale [WSAS]). Interpretation bias at T1 was the hypothesized mechanism. Analysis was performed using a modified intention-to-treat approach.

Results: A total of 268 participants were randomized (mean [SD] age 33.7 [3.9] years; 174 [64.9%] married). Anxiety was significantly lower for RELAX participants vs UC (mean GAD-7 difference, -1.5; 95% CI, -2.4 to -0.6; P = .001). Depression (mean PHQ-9 difference, -0.8; 95% CI -1.5 to -0.1; and mean EPDS difference, -1.1; 95% CI, -2.0 to -0.2), RNT (mean RTQ-10 difference, -2.7; 95% CI, -4.5 to -0.9), worry (mean PSWQ difference, -3.6; 95% CI, -5.9 to -1.3), and perinatal anxiety (mean PASS difference, -5.5; 95% CI, -8.2 to -2.8) were significantly lower at T2. Effects on general anxiety (mean GAD-7 difference, -1.0; 95% CI, -1.9 to -0.1), postnatal depression (mean EPDS difference, -1.3; 95% CI, -2.4 to -0.2), and RNT (mean RTQ-10 difference, -2.4; 95% CI, -4.6 to -0.2) were sustained at T3. RELAX promoted more positive interpretations vs UC (mean difference, 2.1; 95% CI, 1.8-2.3) that did not mediate effects at T2 (indirect effect on GAD-7, -0.2; percentile bootstrap 95% CI, -0.4 to 0.1). Functioning did not differ at T2 (mean WSAS difference, -1.0; 95% CI, -2.5 to 0.5) or T3 (mean WSAS difference, -0.8; 95% CI, -2.7 to 1.2), nor did perinatal anxiety (mean PASS difference, -2.1; 95% CI, -5.5 to 1.4), general depression (mean PHQ-9 difference, -0.2; 95% CI, -1.2 to 0.9), or worry (mean PSWQ difference, -1.4; 95% CI, -4.1 to 1.3) at T3.

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial, anxiety was lower during pregnancy and postnatally for RELAX plus UC participants compared with those receiving UC. Integrating RELAX into maternity care for those at risk of increased anxiety has potential to improve maternal mental health.

item.description:
Importance: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used to support maternal health, but randomized evidence is limited.

Objective: To evaluate whether access to a generative AI maternal health chatbot improved 12-month maternal health outcomes.

Design, setting, and participants: This 2-group randomized clinical trial enrolled 400 participants from October 2023 to December 2024, with 12-month follow-up completed in December 2025. Participants were recruited online across 49 US states and the District of Columbia. Eligible participants were English-speaking, aged 14 years or older, pregnant or parenting an infant younger than 6 months, and self-identified as members of racial and/or ethnic minoritized groups.

Interventions: Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive access to the chatbot or an active control consisting of monthly children's books.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were anxiety and depression symptoms at 12 months measured using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 and Patient Health Questionnaire-9. Secondary outcomes included emergency department visits, pregnancy-related complications, postpartum care checkups, effective contraception use, and sleep duration.

Results: Among 400 randomized participants, the mean (SD) age was 32.6 (5.1) years; 200 (50%) were parenting an infant at enrollment; and 10 (2%) identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, 80 (20%) Asian, 188 (47%) Black or African American, 57 (14%) multiracial, and 65 (16%) Hispanic or Latino. Higher chatbot engagement was associated with longer sleep duration and higher anxiety scores in exploratory within-group analyses.

item.title: Gestational Age- and Altitude-Specific Hemoglobin Thresholds and Candidate Windows for Preterm Birth
item.description:
Importance: Maternal hemoglobin is a clinically accessible biomarker of preterm birth (PTB) risk, but abnormal thresholds are inconsistent and do not account for variation by gestational age or altitude.

Objectives: To evaluate the association between maternal hemoglobin concentration and PTB across gestational ages and altitudes, including PTB subtype, and to define gestational age-specific, altitude-adapted hemoglobin thresholds and assessment windows.

Design, setting, and participants: This multicenter, retrospective cohort study used a multisource database integrating electronic medical records, preconception examination, and geospatial data from 5 medical centers in Yunnan, China, a region with a marked altitudinal gradient, and consecutively included singleton pregnancies delivered between January 1, 2017, and July 31, 2025.

Exposure: Prepregnancy and prenatal hemoglobin values were assessed. Prenatal measurements were grouped into 2-week intervals (target gestational week ±7 days), with 36 weeks analyzed separately.

Main outcomes and measures: Preterm birth was operationally defined as live birth from 28 weeks 0 days through 36 weeks 6 days of gestation.

Results: Of 141 943 singleton live births among women (mean [SD] maternal age, 29.7 [4.6] years), 12 607 (8.88%) were PTBs. Maternal hemoglobin measurement showed a gestational age-dependent U-shaped association with PTB, and thresholds varied across gestation. Compared with the intermediate group, a low hemoglobin concentration measured at 13 weeks (<12.00 g/dL; adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 1.46; 95% CI, 1.17-1.80) was associated with PTB, persisting from 27 weeks onward (<11.00 g/dL; AOR, 1.48; 95% CI, 1.25-1.74). A high hemoglobin concentration from 19 weeks onward was associated with PTB (>13.50 g/dL; AOR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.04-1.55). At high altitude, thresholds were generally higher, and a low hemoglobin concentration from 21 weeks was persistently associated with PTB. Subtype analyses showed earlier low hemoglobin concentration associations for medically indicated PTB and middle- to late-pregnancy high hemoglobin concentration associations for both subtypes.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, hemoglobin thresholds associated with PTB varied across gestation and were generally higher at high altitude; low- and high-hemoglobin assessment windows differed and varied by altitude. These findings may help refine gestational age- and altitude-specific interpretation of routine hemoglobin measurements and PTB risk assessment, pending external validation.

item.title: Overall Survival in Adults With Acute Myeloid Leukemia Initiating Quizartinib vs Midostaurin With Chemotherapy
item.description:
Importance: Midostaurin and quizartinib are approved with intensive chemotherapy (IC) in patients with newly diagnosed FLT3 internal tandem duplication (ITD)-positive acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but no randomized clinical trials have directly compared them.

Objective: To compare 1-year overall survival (OS) among patients with FLT3-ITD variant AML initiating IC with midostaurin or quizartinib.

Design, setting, and participants: This multicenter, retrospective cohort study included patients with newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD variant AML treated at 12 US referral centers between January 1, 2018, and May 31, 2025. Data analysis was performed from January 2026 to August 2026.

Exposures: Induction therapy with IC plus midostaurin or quizartinib.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was 1-year overall survival (OS). Secondary outcomes included 1-year event-free survival (EFS), induction response, and hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) rates at first remission; FLT3 clearance after induction was exploratory. Safety outcomes included rates of febrile neutropenia, infections, intensive care unit use, total parenteral nutrition and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor use, discharge to a rehabilitation facility after index hospitalization, and early mortality. Cox proportional hazards regression models were adjusted for baseline covariates and HCT as time dependent.

Results: Among 215 patients (median [IQR] age, 56.0 [45.0-65.0] years; 119 [55.3%] female), 127 (59.1%) received midostaurin and 88 (40.9%) received quizartinib. Median (IQR) follow-up was 667.0 (289.0-1368.0) days for midostaurin and 324.0 (168.0-546.5) days for quizartinib, reflecting the latter's more recent approval. One-year OS was 78.0% for midostaurin and 93.0% for quizartinib (hazard ratio [HR], 0.22; 95% CI, 0.08-0.58; P = .002). The 1-year EFS was 56.0% for midostaurin and 77.0% for quizartinib (HR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.25-0.74; P = .003). Patients receiving quizartinib had higher rates of composite complete remission (75 [85.2%] vs 93 [73.2%]; P = .03), whereas rates of FLT3 clearance after induction (20 [38.5%] for quizartinib vs 27 [40.3%] for midostaurin; P = .84) and HCT in first remission (47 [53.4%] for quizartinib vs 83 [65.4%] for midostaurin; P = .08) were comparable. Midostaurin was associated with higher intensive care unit use (19 [15.0%] vs 4 [4.5%]; P = .02), discharge to a rehabilitation facility (9 [7.1%] vs 1 [1.1%]; P = .04), and treatment interruptions (32 [25.2%] vs 10 [11.4%]; P = .01). A sensitivity analysis limited to patients treated in 2023 or later (more balanced follow-up) showed directionally consistent but nonsignificant OS and EFS differences.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of adults with FLT3-ITD variant AML, IC plus quizartinib was associated with improved 1-year survival, induction response, and safety compared with IC plus midostaurin.

item.title: Body Mass Index, Genetic Predisposition, and Obesity-Related Second Cancer Risk in Cancer Survivors
item.description:
Importance: Excess body weight is an established risk factor for second primary cancers (SPCs) among cancer survivors. Whether genetic susceptibility to higher body mass index (BMI) is associated with the risk of obesity-related SPCs remains unclear.

Objective: To examine associations of genetic predisposition to higher BMI with the risk of obesity-related SPCs and its joint association with BMI.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective cohort study used data from the Cancer Prevention Study II Nutrition Cohort, a large prospective study of adults residing in 21 states in the US who were cancer-free at the time of the 1992 survey and responded to biennial follow-up questionnaires starting in 1997. Response rates to the biennial questionnaires ranged from 78.1% to 92.1%. Participants for this analysis included cancer survivors who received a diagnosis of a first primary, nonmetastatic invasive cancer between 1992 and 2015, provided a biospecimen sample, and were followed up through 2017. Analyses were conducted between September 2025 and August 2026.

Exposures: A polygenic score for BMI (PGS-BMI) and BMI.

Main outcomes and measures: Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate associations between PGS-BMI and obesity-related SPC risk, as well as between BMI and obesity-related SPC risk stratified by PGS-BMI tertiles.

Results: This analysis included 14 309 cancer survivors. Their median (IQR) age at first cancer diagnosis was 72.9 (68.2-77.4) years. Approximately 58.6% (8378) of survivors were male, and 58.6% (8382) had a BMI in the overweight (25 to <30) or obese (≥30) range. During a median (IQR) follow-up of 9.1 (4.6-14.2) years, there were 722 (5.0%) obesity-related SPCs. Compared with survivors in the lowest PGS-BMI tertile, those in the highest tertile had greater risk of obesity-related SPCs (hazard ratio [HR], 1.26 [95% CI, 1.06-1.51]). Obesity was associated with increased risk across tertiles of the PGS-BMI without evidence of interaction (P = .89 for interaction). Compared with survivors with low genetic predisposition and BMI lower than 25, those with low genetic predisposition and obesity had higher obesity-related SPC risk (HR, 1.59 [95% CI, 1.21-2.09]) and those with high genetic predisposition and obesity had the highest risk (HR, 1.82 [95% CI, 1.38-2.40]). The 10-year cumulative incidence ranged from 3.4% (95% CI, 2.9%-4.0%) to 5.1% (95% CI, 4.3%-5.9%) across joint exposure groups.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of cancer survivors, genetic susceptibility to higher BMI was associated with a modestly increased risk of obesity-related SPCs, whereas obesity was associated with greater risk regardless of genetic predisposition. These findings underscore the importance of weight management for all cancer survivors and suggest that a meaningful proportion of obesity-related SPCs may be preventable.

item.description:
Importance: Although external validation of machine learning (ML)-based delirium risk models is a key stage in the model development pipeline, few published reports exist. Moreover, ML-based delirium risk models commonly degrade in performance during external validation.

Objective: To examine the performance of a fusion multimodal with natural language processing (NLP) delirium risk stratification model in live clinical practice with cross-hospital external validation.

Design, setting, and participants: This quality improvement study evaluated live clinical deployment of the model among patients 60 years or older who were admitted to non-intensive care units at Mount Sinai Hospital (MSH), with external validation performed at Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital (MSM), from December 1, 2024, to December 31, 2025.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were performance of the risk stratification model, assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and monthly delirium detection rates. A 2 × 2 confusion matrix was created, and the 4 cells were used to calculate model performance metrics and compare associated diagnostic yield between premodel deployment and active model deployment periods.

Results: The overall sample included 33 095 admissions to non-intensive care units at MSM and MSH (mean [SD] age, 74.86 (9.22) years; 15 601 women [47.1%], 17 271 men [52.2%]). A total of 9020 MSM inpatient admissions were assigned a delirium risk score by the risk stratification model during live clinical operations and were compared to 21 186 MSH inpatient admissions that were assigned a risk score by the same model. Age at admission significantly differed between patients at MSM and MSH (MSM: median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years vs MSH: 72.62 [66.64-79.65] years; P < .001). Patients from MSM and MSH also significantly differed by sex, race and ethnicity, surgical vs medical primary diagnosis, length of stay, and dementia prevalence rate. Among 11 909 MSM patients, patients in the pre-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 78.00 [71.00-85.00] years) were significantly older than those in the post-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years) (P < .001). The AUROC of the model was 0.91 (95% CI, 0.90-0.92) for MSM and 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93-0.94) for MSH. The positive predictive value of the model was 25.9% for MSM and 19.4% for MSH. For MSM, the mean monthly delirium detection rate significantly increased from 9.23% (95% CI, 8.07%-10.38%) to 19.59% (95% CI, 17.32%-21.85%) after model deployment (P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this quality improvement study, an ML-based delirium risk stratification model maintained acceptable discriminative performance during external deployment without retraining and was similar to its performance at the development site without retraining. Model deployment was also associated with increased diagnostic yield but a high false positive rate. These findings provide further evidence of the potential generalizability of the model.

item.title: Managing Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth in Pediatric Short Bowel Syndrome: A Consensus Statement
item.description:
Importance: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is a common and clinically important complication of short bowel syndrome (SBS) in children, contributing to feeding intolerance, malabsorption, bloodstream infections, and frequent antibiotic exposure. Diagnostic and management practices vary widely across centers, and no rigorously developed, evidence-informed pediatric-specific guidance currently exists.

Objective: To develop international, pediatric-specific, expert consensus recommendations for the diagnosis and management of SIBO in children with SBS, with emphasis on diagnostic approach, antibiotic therapy, treatment response, and prevention.

Evidence review: A modified Delphi process was conducted between April 4, 2024, and February 18, 2025. A 7-member steering committee reviewed pediatric and adult SIBO literature using the terms small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth, short bowel syndrome, intestinal failure, and pediatric. Because pediatric-specific data were limited and study designs were heterogeneous, systematic reviews and meta-analyses were not feasible. Fifty-five international experts from multidisciplinary intestinal rehabilitation programs in North America and Europe were invited to participate in 3 rounds of anonymous online surveys and 2 in-person moderated consensus meetings. Draft statements were iteratively refined. Consensus was defined a priori as agreement of 75% or greater among respondents.

Findings: Completed surveys were received from 33 participants in round 1, 38 in round 2, and 28 in round 3. Consensus was achieved on 21 statements involving diagnostic approaches, therapeutic strategies, and monitoring practices. Recommendations addressed the use of breath testing and clinical criteria, indications for empiric antibiotic therapy and cycling, antibiotic selection and duration, and dietary considerations. Symptomatic improvement was considered an acceptable indicator of treatment response. Metronidazole was identified as the preferred first-line antibiotic, and long-term antibiotic cycling was supported for selected patients with recurrent, treatment-responsive SIBO. Collectively, the statements provide a practical framework to support consistent clinical decision-making in pediatric SBS-associated SIBO.

Conclusions and relevance: This Delphi-based consensus provides the first international pediatric-specific guidance for diagnosing and managing SIBO in children with SBS. Implementation of these recommendations may reduce practice variability, support more judicious antibiotic use, and improve patient outcomes while establishing a foundation for future research in this high-risk population.

item.description:
Importance: Conventional approaches to analyzing composite end points in clinical trials may not fully capture clinically meaningful treatment effects.

Objective: To estimate treatment effects of early metformin initiation on clinically ordered glycemic outcomes (insulin initiation and fasting hyperglycemia at gestational weeks 32 and 38) using generalized pairwise comparisons (GPCs).

Design, setting, and participants: This secondary analysis of a double-masked, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial (conducted from June 2017 through September 2022) at 2 centers in Ireland (1 tertiary hospital and 1 regional hospital) included participants with gestational diabetes based on World Health Organization 2013 criteria. Participants were followed up through 12 weeks post partum. The data analysis was performed between October 18, 2025, and February 2, 2026.

Intervention: Participants were randomized 1:1 to metformin (maximum dose, 2500 mg) or matching placebo, in addition to usual care.

Main outcomes and measures: Generalized pairwise comparisons were performed using (1) a prioritized hierarchy (insulin initiation, fasting hyperglycemia at week 32, and fasting hyperglycemia at week 38) and (2) nonprioritized analyses of each end point, with overall summaries using equal weights and prespecified clinical weights (0.50, 0.25, and 0.25, respectively). Treatment effect sizes were summarized using win ratio (WR), net treatment benefit (NTB), and win odds (WO).

Results: Of 535 randomized pregnancies, 526 (262 placebo [49.0%] and 264 metformin [51.0%]; mean [SD] age of participants, 34.4 [4.8] years) had primary outcome data. Prioritized GPCs favored metformin over placebo for the composite outcome (WR, 1.46 [95% CI, 1.13-1.89]; NTB, 13.7 percentage points [95% CI, 4.3-22.8 percentage points]; WO, 1.34 [95% CI, 1.10-1.64]) (P = .004). The largest separation was observed for insulin initiation (WR, 1.68 [95% CI, 1.19-2.38]; NTB, 12.7 percentage points [95% CI, 4.2-21.0 percentage points]) (P = .003). Nonprioritized overall summaries favored metformin (WR, 1.53 [95% CI, 1.16-2.01]; NTB, 7.5 percentage points [95% CI, 2.7-12.3 percentage points]; WO, 1.32 [95% CI, 1.10-1.57]) (P = .002), with consistent clinically weighted results (WR, 1.57 [95% CI, 1.19-2.08]; NTB, 8.8 percentage points [95% CI, 3.4-14.2 percentage points]; WO, 1.39 [95% CI, 1.14-1.70]) (P = .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial, prioritized and nonprioritized GPCs yielded statistically significant overall estimates favoring early metformin initiation over placebo across insulin initiation and fasting hyperglycemia outcomes. These findings complement the original primary analysis, provide a more clinically interpretable assessment of the composite outcome, and may inform prospective end point design in future trials.

item.title: Spousal Traumatic Brain Injury and Risk of Mortality, Dementia, and Cardiovascular Events
item.description:
Importance: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is highly prevalent in older adults. While there is strong and growing evidence that TBI is associated with caregiver burden and psychological health, it remains unclear whether a spouse's TBI is associated with the long-term health of the uninjured partner.

Objective: To evaluate whether having a spouse who sustains an incident TBI is associated with risk of mortality, dementia, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and to assess whether associations differ by sex or survival of the injured spouse after TBI.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective community-based cohort of married couples was performed at 4 US centers in North Carolina, Mississippi, Minnesota, and Maryland as part of the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) Study. Of 4506 baseline spousal pairs, 3281 were retained for mortality and dementia analyses and 2740 of these for MACE analyses. Participants contributed person-time from baseline (1987-1989) until incident outcome, death, loss to follow-up, divorce or separation, or administrative censoring on December 31, 2022. Analyses were conducted from November 24, 2025, through August 25, 2026.

Exposure: Incident spousal TBI (ascertained using self-report, hospitalization surveillance, and linked Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services data), modeled as a 2-category time-varying exposure (spousal TBI vs no spousal TBI) and 4-category exposure incorporating spousal death.

Main outcomes and measures: Incident all-cause mortality, dementia, and MACE. Cox proportional hazards regression shared frailty models were used to estimate associations adjusted for demographic, clinical, and behavioral characteristics.

Results: Among 3281 married pairs included in mortality and dementia analyses (among whom, 2740 pairs were included in MACE analyses), the mean (SD) age at baseline was 54.5 (5.5) years, with 3281 female and 3281 male spouses (for a total of 6562 participants). The median follow-up was 19.5 (IQR, 10.6-29.0) years. Spousal TBI was associated with increased risk of mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 1.24 [95% CI, 1.07-1.43]; P = .004) but not dementia (HR, 1.17 [95% CI, 0.88-1.56]; P = .28) or MACE (HR, 1.15 [95% CI, 0.84-1.57]; P = .40). In sex-stratified analyses, associations were similar among males and females. In models incorporating spousal death, mortality risk was higher among individuals whose spouse was alive with a TBI (HR, 1.22 [95% CI, 1.05-1.41]; P = .008), higher among those whose spouse was deceased without a TBI (HR, 1.48 [95% CI, 1.36-1.61]; P < .001), and higher among those whose spouse was deceased with a TBI (HR, 1.27 [95% CI, 1.07-1.52]; P = .006) compared with those whose spouse was alive without a TBI. Results were similar, but less precise, for dementia and MACE.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of married pairs of participants in the ARIC Study, having a spouse who sustained a TBI was associated with a modest but significantly higher risk of mortality in the uninjured partner, whereas findings for dementia and major adverse cardiovascular events were less consistent. These findings suggest that the consequences of TBI may extend beyond injured individuals and support family- and care partner-centered approaches to care.

item.title: Noninpatient Alternative Treatment Venues for Acute Care Needs
item.description:
Importance: Hospitalizations are costly and may lead to adverse events. Some health systems offer treatment in alternative venues of care for select patients.

Objective: To describe use and short-term outcomes of emergency department (ED) patients transitioned to noninpatient care settings (ambulatory treatment center [ATC], advanced care at home [ACAH], or emergency department observation unit [EDOU]) compared with inpatient care.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study of ED patients aged 19 years or older was conducted from January 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025, at multisite community ED and inpatient medical centers within an integrated delivery system (Kaiser Permanente Northern California). Included patients had active health plan membership; had an ED visit for heart failure, pneumonia, cellulitis, urinary tract infection, COVID-19, or anemia; and had their care transitioned to an ATC, ACAH program (Kaiser Permanente Advanced Care at Home), EDOU, or inpatient bed.

Exposure: Treatment venue.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes were care escalation (inpatient admission) for patients treated in an ATC, ACAH program, or EDOU, as well as 7-day ED return visits, 30-day hospitalizations, and 30-day mortality following care completion across all venues. Unadjusted outcome rates are reported.

Results: This study included 26 618 ED encounters (median patient age, 77 years [IQR, 65-85 years]; 52.6% female). Among 22 755 unique patients, 87.4% had 1 encounter, 9.8% had 2 encounters, and 2.8% had more than 2 encounters. There were 728 (2.7%), 880 (3.3%), 5133 (19.3%), and 19 877 (74.7%) encounters in ATC, ACAH, EDOU, and hospital settings, respectively. One-quarter of patients (25.3%) received care in an ATC, ACAH program, or EDOU. Inpatient admission rates were lower for ATC and ACAH encounters than for EDOU encounters (4.3% [95% CI, 2.7%-5.8%], 5.3% [3.8%-6.8%], and 28.0% [26.8%-29.2%], respectively). Rates of 7-day ED visits were similar across venues (ATC: 10.4% [95% CI, 7.8%-12.9%]; ACAH: 5.3% [3.8%-6.8%]; EDOU: 9.2% [8.4%-10.0%]; and hospital: 8.5% [8.1%-8.9%]). In contrast, 30-day mortality and hospitalization rates were lower among ATC, ACAH, and EDOU encounters than in hospital encounters (30-day mortality: 2.1% [95% CI, 1.0%-3.2%], 1.7% [0.8%-2.6%], 2.8% [2.3%-3.2%], and 5.3% [5.0%-5.6%]; and 30-day hospitalization: 11.4% [95% CI, 8.8%-14.1%], 8.3% [6.3%-10.2%], 12.7% [11.7%-13.7%], and 15.3% [14.7%-15.8%], respectively).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of patients treated in alternative venues of care, one-quarter received care in an ATC, ACAH program, or EDOU. These findings suggest that adoption of novel treatment spaces for appropriately selected patients may allow health systems to focus hospital resources on the patients with the most complex needs.

item.title: Accelerated Approvals and Clinical Evidence for Medications for Children
item.description:
Importance: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) accelerated approval (AA) pathway allows early access to therapies for serious or life-threatening diseases based on surrogate end points reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. In pediatrics, where evidence generation is challenging, the use and performance of this pathway remain underexamined.

Objective: To characterize preapproval and postapproval studies of drugs granted pediatric AAs.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study identified preapproval and postapproval studies for pediatric AAs granted between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2020. Study characteristics and regulatory outcomes were extracted using publicly available sources, including FDA product labels, approval letters, the postmarketing requirements (PMRs) database, ClinicalTrials.gov, and matched peer-reviewed publications as of August 22, 2026.

Exposures: Granting of pediatric AA.

Main outcomes and measures: Study characteristics and regulatory outcomes, including time from AA to traditional approval.

Results: From 2000 to 2020, the FDA granted AA to 26 drugs for 35 pediatric indications (7 pediatric-only, 6 pediatric extension, and 22 combined pediatric-adult). Most approvals were supported by extrapolation, including pharmacokinetic bridging. A total of 47 PMRs were issued, primarily for efficacy verification (28 [59.6%]), 26 (55.3%) of which were fulfilled, contributing to traditional approval for 22 indications (62.9%) after a median of 58.1 (IQR, 44.5-80.1) months. Postapproval studies enrolled more patients than preapproval studies (median, 125 [IQR, 58-304] vs 55 [IQR, 27-119]; P = .004) but maintained enrollment of fewer pediatric patients (median, 11 [IQR, 0-61] vs 13 [0-33]; P = .93). Pediatric-only indications had the longest conversion times and lowest PMR fulfillment rates, accounting for 3 of 4 cases with delayed PMR fulfillment.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of pediatric AAs between 2000 and 2020, approval frequently relied on surrogate end points and extrapolation with pharmacokinetic bridging studies, with limited pediatric enrollment. Although confirmatory studies typically verified efficacy within 4 years, pediatric-only indications experienced persistent delays, underscoring ongoing challenges in timely pediatric evidence generation.

item.title: National Trends in Severe Maternal Morbidity by Insurance and Race and Ethnicity
item.description:
Importance: Rates of severe maternal morbidity (SMM) and mortality are rising in the US, disproportionally affecting racial and ethnic minority groups and Medicaid beneficiaries. Contemporary analyses investigating the intersectional impact of insurance and race and ethnicity on SMM are lacking.

Objective: To examine national trends in SMM and maternal mortality across deliveries and evaluate the intersectional association of insurance type and race and ethnicity with these outcomes.

Design, setting, and participants: This serial cross-sectional study used population-based National Inpatient Sample (a 20% stratified sample of hospital discharges) data on delivery hospitalizations from October 1, 2015, to December 31, 2022, in the US, with analyses completed between July 7, 2025, and January 30, 2026.

Exposure: Assessment of insurance (private vs Medicaid) and race and ethnicity independently and cross-classified into 10 intersectional groups.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were composite SMM, nontransfusion-only SMM, and mortality. Multivariable logistic regression was used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (AORs) for outcomes across insurance, race and ethnicity, and intersectional groups.

Results: Among 27 341 986 weighted deliveries (mean [SD] maternal age, 29.0 [5.8] years; 6.3% of Asian or Pacific Islander, 16.2% of Black, 22.4% of Hispanic, 0.8% of Native American, and 54.3% of White race and ethnicity), 563 250 (2.1%) were complicated by SMM, 2320 of which (0.4%) resulted in death. From 2015 to 2022, composite SMM rates increased 40.5% (from 175.0 to 245.9 per 10 000 deliveries; P < .001), with 16 of 21 individual complications (76.2%) significantly increasing. Medicaid covered 11 658 119 weighted deliveries (45.5%), and included a greater proportion of Black, Hispanic, and Native American individuals than the privately insured population. Adjusted odds of composite SMM were elevated among all intersectional groups compared with White patients with private insurance (all P < .001). Within each racial and ethnic group, SMM odds were significantly higher with Medicaid vs private insurance (Asian or Pacific Islander: AOR, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.20-1.36]; Black: AOR, 1.13 [95% CI, 1.10-1.17]; Hispanic: AOR, 1.29 [95% CI, 1.24-1.34]; Native American: AOR, 1.44 [95% CI, 1.24-1.67]; White: AOR, 1.23 [95% CI, 1.20-1.26]). Significantly increased odds of mortality were primarily observed for Medicaid-insured Asian or Pacific Islander (AOR, 2.63 [95% CI, 1.25-5.52]), Hispanic (AOR, 1.97 [95% CI, 1.16-3.35]), and White (AOR, 2.15 [95% CI, 1.55-2.99]) patients but not for Medicaid-insured Black patients (AOR, 1.55 [95% CI, 0.99-2.41]).

Conclusions and relevance: This serial cross-sectional study of births in the US found that racial and ethnic minority status was independently associated with elevated odds of SMM. Medicaid enrollment further compounded this risk and was associated with maternal mortality, suggesting underlying structural inequities that accompany Medicaid coverage rather than a direct effect of insurance type. Addressing these structural barriers through policy reform, including equitable reimbursement and expanded preconception coverage, is critical to mitigate these maternal health inequities.

item.title: Full-Service Mobile Food Markets and Dietary Quality in Low-Income Housing Communities: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Full-service mobile markets, also known as grocery stores on wheels, may improve diet-related outcomes by bringing low-cost, nutritious food to individuals experiencing low incomes and low food access.

Objective: To determine the impact of the full-service Twin Cities Mobile Market on dietary outcomes in low-income communities.

Design, setting, participants: This cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted over 3 waves (January 2022 to October 2025) across 12 public or private subsidized housing sites in the Minneapolis-St. Paul, Minnesota, area. Participants were screened for interest in the mobile market. Follow-up assessments began after 6 months of market service. Analyses were finalized September 2026.

Intervention: Sites were randomized to weekly market service or waiting list control groups.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcome: diet quality (Healthy Eating Index-2020 via 24-hour recalls). A priori secondary outcomes: dietary intake (fruit and vegetable, energy, sodium, and percentage of calories from added sugar), food security (18-item US Department of Agriculture Food Security Screening Module), and fruit and vegetable servings procured for the home (validated tracking tool). Adjusted intention-to-treat (ITT) generalized estimating equations were used to assess outcome differences between treatment groups.

Results: Among 262 adults who enrolled in the mobile market study, 242 participants (mean [SD] age, 66.5 [11.5] years; 156 women [64.5%]) across 12 sites completed baseline assessments and were randomized to mobile market service or waiting list control groups. There were 137 individuals (56.6%) who received Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits. Sites had a mean (SD) of 18.2 (4.4) weekly transactions (mean of 110 of 1071 households [10.3%]). Of 109 intervention site participants, 47 individuals (43.1%) shopped at the mobile market 1 or more times in implementation months 5 to 6, while 90 of 94 individuals who reported ever using the market (95.7%) reported that they would recommend the market service. Participant retention was 218 of 242 participants (90.0%). In ITT models, the primary outcome of diet quality (adjusted mean difference, 1.25 [95% CI, -1.60 to 4.10]) among 215 participants and 6 of 7 secondary outcomes (fruit and vegetable, energy, and added sugar intake; food security and food security improvement; fruit and vegetable procurement) were not significantly different between groups. Intervention site participants consumed an adjusted mean difference of 397 mg (95% CI, -636 to -158 mg) less sodium daily compared with participants in the waiting list control group. Main findings were consistent across 4 sensitivity and supplemental analyses, except the per-protocol sensitivity analysis, which found that participants in the intervention group consumed an adjusted mean difference of 2.35% (95% CI, 0.66%-4.04%) more calories from added sugar compared with the control group.

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, satisfaction with the mobile market was high, but the mobile market did not improve diet quality or most outcomes examined. The mobile market was associated with a meaningful sodium reduction that could improve population-level health.

item.title: Caring Contacts and Suicidality Among American Indian and Alaska Native Communities: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: For American Indian and Alaska Native communities, connectedness and belonging are strengths that may reduce suicide risk.

Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of culturally-adapted Caring Contacts combined with optimal available resources (intervention) compared with optimal available resources alone (control) in reducing suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and suicide-related hospitalizations.

Design, setting, and participants: The CARE study was a blinded, 2-group randomized clinical trial conducted between May 2018 and September 2023 among 5 American Indian and Alaska Native communities in Alaska, the Northern Plains, and the Southern Plains, including 4 tribal communities and 1 tribal health organization. Participants were English-speaking adults (age ≥18 years) self-identifying as American Indian or Alaska Native with active suicidality. Analysis was conducted January through April 2024.

Intervention: Caring Contacts is a low-cost intervention via brief, nondemanding messages exclusively focused on expressing care and interest sent by text message or greeting card on a pre-determined schedule over 12 months.

Main outcomes and measures: Outcomes included suicidal ideation in the past month (measured using the Suicidal Ideation Questionnaire-Junior [SIQ-Jr]), number of suicide attempts, and suicide-related hospitalizations over 12 months. Retention of active suicidality at follow-up was added as an additional outcome.

Results: Of 1390 individuals prescreened for eligibility, 1202 consented and were screened for eligibility, and 709 (457 [64.5%] female; mean [SD] age, 35.4 [11.5] years) were enrolled and randomized, including 357 participants in the control group and 352 participants in the Caring Contacts intervention. Most participants (549 [77.4%]) self-identified as American Indian or Alaska Native only, and 160 participants (22.6%) as American Indian or Alaska Native plus another racial group. More than half of participants (392 [55.3%]) were never married. The mean (SD) SIQ-Jr score at baseline was 42.0 (13.8), and 604 participants (85.2%) had ever made a suicide attempt. Overall, 454 participants (64.0%) provided 12-month follow-up data. Between baseline and the 12-month follow-up, both groups showed significant reductions in suicidal ideation (mean [SD] score: Caring Contacts, 41.4 [13.7] vs 22.7 [15.3]; enhanced usual care, 42.5 [13.9] vs 23.1 [14.5]) and participants with a past-year suicide attempt (Caring Contacts, 169 of 352 participants [48.0%] vs 34/240 participants [14.2%]; enhanced usual care 155 of 357 participants [43.4%] vs 39 of 238 participants [16.4%]); however, no statistically significant between-group differences were found.

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial of culturally adapted Caring Contacts among American Indian or Alaska Native adults with active suicidality, Caring Contacts did not improve suicidal outcomes beyond optimal available resources alone. Similar improvements in both groups may reflect regression to the mean, the therapeutic impact of compassionate baseline engagement with supportive community staff, or the active components of optimal available resources. Further research should explore these dynamics and other culturally grounded interventions.

item.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Remote Symptom Monitoring During Adjuvant Endocrine Therapy in Breast Cancer
item.description:
Importance: Adjuvant endocrine therapy (AET) reduces recurrence and mortality for women with early-stage hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, yet long-term adherence is suboptimal, largely due to treatment-related symptoms. Remote patient monitoring (RPM) is a potential strategy to improve symptom management, but evidence of its cost-effectiveness is limited.

Objective: To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of RPM for women prescribed AET for early-stage breast cancer.

Design, setting, and participants: This economic evaluation used data from the THRIVE trial, which randomized adult women initiating AET to an application (app), the app with tailored feedback, or enhanced usual care (EUC) at a large cancer center with 14 clinics from November 15, 2018, to June 11, 2021. The intervention lasted 6 months, and participants were followed up for 12 months (completed September 19, 2022). Each of the 2 interventions was compared with EUC, with uncertainty assessed using probabilistic sensitivity analyses. Data analyses were performed from February 1, 2025, to September 2, 2026.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes included costs, which were captured during the 12-month study period from a societal perspective, including medical costs, patient time and travel costs, clinician time costs responding to alerts, and app costs; quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), derived from patient-reported 12-item Short Form Health Survey scores; incremental cost-effectiveness ratios; and incremental net monetary benefit.

Results: Of 304 participants randomized, 214 had complete data. The mean (SD) age was 58.9 (10.8) years. Mean (SD) total costs were highest for the EUC arm ($11 596.10 [$30 231.95]) compared with the app arm ($6682.15 [$12 963.34]; difference, -$4913.95 [95% CI, -$12 864.27 to $3036.37]) and app plus feedback arm ($11 407.85 [$47 068.42]; difference, -$188.25 [95% CI, -$12 830.16 to $12 453.66]). The mean (SD) estimated QALYs were similar across arms (app, 0.79 [012]; app plus feedback, 0.78 [0.13]; EUC, 0.78 [0.12]). This results in an incremental net monetary benefit of $5813.95 (95% uncertainty interval [UI], -$1860.00 to $16 492.58) for app group and $88.25 (95% UI, -$14 781.73 to $13 849.34) for the app plus feedback group at $100 000 per QALY. Probabilistic sensitivity analyses suggest that the app intervention had a 68.2% to 78.1% probability of being cost-effective compared with EUC across a willingness-to-pay threshold of $0 to $200 000 per QALY, while the app plus feedback intervention had a 53.6% to 70.8% probability of being cost-effective.

Conclusions and relevance: In this economic evaluation of RPM for women receiving AET, app-only RPM showed lower costs with similar QALY compared with EUC. Its simpler design may also be more readily scalable than the app plus feedback intervention, supporting its potential as a pragmatic, value-based supportive care strategy in oncology.

item.title: Protein Biomarkers of Lung Cancer Risk Among Individuals Who Never Smoked
item.description:
Importance: Approximately one-quarter of lung cancers occur in people who never smoked (PWNS). For smoking-associated lung cancer, blood-based protein biomarkers can improve risk assessment.

Objective: To identify protein biomarkers for lung cancer among PWNS.

Design, setting, and participants: This nested case-control study from 4 cohorts in the Lung Cancer Cohort Consortium (LC3) was conducted for discovery to identify proteins, and a cohort study was conducted using data in the UK Biobank for replication. Participants were from the US, China, and the United Kingdom and donated blood samples between 1996 and 2010. Lung cancer case-control pairs of PWNS from 4 cohorts in the LC3 were matched by cohort, age, sex, and blood collection date. In addition, 49 291 participants in the UK Biobank were included. Data were analyzed from March 2024 to May 2025.

Exposure: A total of 2821 circulating proteins measured in prediagnostic blood samples collected up to 5 years before lung cancer diagnosis for cases.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary measures were odds ratios (ORs) for discovery and hazard ratios (HRs) for replication.

Results: Among 180 case-control pairs of PWNS (360 participants) in the 4 LC3 cohorts, 256 participants (71.1%) were female, and the median (IQR) age at enrollment was 66 (55-70) years. In LC3, using a false discovery rate-adjusted P value threshold of .05, 2 proteins were identified as being associated with lung cancer among PWNS: carcinoembryonic antigen-related cell adhesion molecule 5 (CEACAM5) (OR, 1.65 [95% CI, 1.31-2.09]) and CEACAM6 (OR, 1.72 [95% CI, 1.33-2.22]). Associations for both proteins were successfully replicated among participants analyzed regardless of smoking history across 5 years of follow-up in the UK Biobank (CEACAM5: HR, 1.92 [95% CI, 1.66-2.22]; CEACAM6: HR, 1.86 [95% CI,1.59-2.16]). The correlation between CEACAM5 and CEACAM6 was weak (Pearson ρ = 0.25 in the LC3); therefore, both proteins maintained associations with high relative risks after mutual adjustment. For 36 proteins previously identified as robust markers of smoking-related lung cancer, most showed no evidence of an association among PWNS (median OR, 1.47 [IQR, 1.38-1.61] vs 1.01 [IQR, 0.94-1.13] in smoking-related vs nonsmoking lung cancer).

Conclusions and relevance: In this nested case-control study, 2 proteins were identified, CEACAM5 and CEACAM6, that were associated with lung cancer in PWNS. Larger studies are needed to evaluate whether there are additional biomarkers associated with lung cancer in PWNS and whether they can identify PWNS with high lung cancer risk.
